n: Hiram, king of the wealthy Phoenician port of Tyre, sends cedar and skilled workers to build David a palace—international recognition of David’s new kingdom.

f.g: Prized cedar wood from Lebanon, a mark of royal building.

n: David understands that his success comes from the Lord, and that God lifted up his kingdom for the sake of His people—not merely for David’s glory.

f.g: A reminder that leadership exists to bless the people, not the leader.

n: David takes more wives in Jerusalem and has more children. The law warned kings against multiplying wives, and the Book of Mormon and D&C speak to David’s marriages as well.
David’s children born in Jerusalem are named, including Nathan and Solomon, both ancestors of Jesus in the Gospel genealogies.
More of David’s sons born in Jerusalem.
Three more sons, matching the list in chapter 3.
The list closes. Beeliada (“the Lord knows”) is called Eliada elsewhere, perhaps because “Baal” (“lord”) later became associated with idolatry.

f.g: “The Lord knows”; called Eliada in 1 Chronicles 3:8 and 2 Samuel 5:16.

n: When the Philistines hear that David is king over all Israel, they march out to crush him before he grows stronger.

f.g: Came looking for him to attack.

n: They spread out in the valley of Rephaim, just southwest of Jerusalem.
Unlike Saul, David first asks God for guidance. The Lord tells him to go, promising victory. Seeking the Lord is the secret of David’s success in Chronicles.
David wins and says God burst through his enemies like a flood breaking through a dam. The place is named Baal-perazim, “Lord of breakthroughs.”

f.w: like the breaking forth of waters

n: The fleeing Philistines leave their idols behind, and David orders them burned, as the law of Moses commanded.
The Philistines regroup and attack again in the same valley.
David asks God again rather than assuming the same plan will work. This time God gives a different strategy: circle around and attack from near the trees.

f.g: He sought fresh guidance for a new situation instead of relying on past success.
Hebrew baka’—probably balsam or poplar trees; the exact tree is uncertain.

n: The signal will be a sound like marching in the treetops—God’s own army going ahead to fight. David is to move when he hears it.

f.w: a sound of going in the tops of the mulberry trees
God is gone forth before thee

n: David obeys exactly, and Israel defeats the Philistines from Gibeon all the way to Gezer.

f.w: David therefore did as God commanded him

f.g: Gezer, a city on the edge of the coastal plain.

n: David’s fame spreads everywhere, and the Lord makes the nations respect and fear him. The chronicler gives God the credit.

f.w: the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations
